lead: Fixating on making the number look good can pull you away from what you actually wanted.
when: When the numbers you're measured on keep improving but user experience, quality, or real ability isn't keeping pace, or when people start working out how to "hit the target."
body:
You want to build a reading habit, so you make a rule: fifty pages a day. At first, the number reminds you to open the book. Later, to meet the quota, you start picking pages with less text and flipping past anything hard to understand. The page count looks great, but your understanding hasn't grown with it.

Goodhart's Law warns that when a measure originally used to track a goal is heavily relied on as a target for evaluation or control, the ways people adapt and optimize for it can weaken its ability to represent the real goal.

Page count was only ever one clue about how your reading was going. Once rewards, evaluation, or your own sense of satisfaction are all tied to it, behavior can start to revolve around the number. Goodhart's Law prompts you to check: when this number improves, is the thing I actually care about improving too?

The problem isn't that every metric is useless; it's treating a stand-in signal as the end goal. Use numbers to spot changes, then judge them together with quality, real feedback, and any side effects, so the metric helps you observe instead of defining everything that matters.

A side-by-side comparison should give "how the number looks" and "the real effect" a place of their own. The two may improve together or drift apart. The point is to check how they're connected, not to assume every number is lying.
example:
A customer support team wants to help users more promptly, so it measures "tickets closed per person per day." Before long, some people close complicated issues too early or ask users to submit them again. The number of closed tickets goes up, yet users' problems may still be unsolved.

Start by spelling out the real goal: users' problems get properly resolved without overly long waits. Then look at whether issues were resolved, whether people had to ask for help again, user feedback, and handling time, and spot-check specific cases. Adding a few more numbers isn't a cure-all either; keep watching how people adapt to the new rules.
extra:
If you treat "how many thinking models I've read" as your learning score, you might quickly mark all 87 entries as read but be unable to say how even one of them applies to real life. The read count records what you've browsed; on its own, it can't prove how much you understand.

Keep the progress bar, but add a small action that's closer to the real goal: pick a model and write an example from your own life, explain it again a few days later with the page closed, or note how you adjusted after actually using it once. What really helps is the change in how you think.
steps: Write the real goal in one sentence, then explain why your current metric represents it and what it might miss.
Think about how someone could improve the number without improving the goal, and actively look for loopholes or likely side effects.
Check the metric against quality feedback and specific cases, allow the rules to be revised, and keep watching whether behavior is being pulled off course.
caution: It isn't a law of physics saying every metric must fail, and it isn't an argument against recording data. Whether a metric is useful depends on the goal, the incentives, the setting, and how it's checked. The popular line "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" is a later, widely circulated paraphrase; it works best as a reminder to check for risks.
exercise: Pick a number you often chase, such as pages read, streak days, or tasks completed. Write down the real goal, describe one situation where the number improves but the goal doesn't, and think of one way to check for it.
brief: A stick figure chases an ever-rising gauge bar while a curved arrow veers away from the real bullseye beside it; another stick figure uses a magnifying glass to check the distance between the metric and the goal.
diagramCaption: On the left, the recorded count rises, while on the right the real effect may stay where it was. Check how the two are connected before deciding whether a better number means the goal was reached.
sources: Michael McIntyre, University of Cambridge · Goodhart's Law and the Origin of Its Wording
